source.title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation

page_placements.theme: Example-specific memorization can help valid rare or difficult examples

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests memorization and its contribution to accuracy with subsampled influence estimates and removal experiments, rather than fitting completely random labels as in the claim's original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on memorization estimates, influence, and test accuracy after removing examples; these bear on V5's generalization clause but it does not test random-label fitting, unstructured inputs, optimization time, smooth corruption levels, or learning order. Its discussion of Arpit et al. is cited prior work, not this study's result.
record.test_reason: The study measures example-level memorization through subsampled self-influence and the accuracy effects of removing training examples. It does not test random-label fitting, corruption trajectories, learning order, or removal of explicit regularization. Removing examples does not test V5's claim about removing regularization. Random-label fitting and regularization results are discussed as prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that memorized training examples can improve accuracy on visually similar test examples, supporting the long-tail theory, and that much of memorization resides in learned representations before the final layer.
record.recipe_differences: Uses subsampled memorization and influence estimates, then removes selected examples and measures accuracy; it does not reproduce random-label fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of removing examples depends on dataset and memorization threshold; the authors state that accuracy effects depend on available example count and data variability.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing memorized or high-influence examples reduces true-label test accuracy. On CIFAR-100, removing high-influence examples reduces overall accuracy by 2.54 ± 0.2 percentage points, with most of that loss concentrated on their influenced test examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Memorizing individual examples from rare subpopulations can improve generalization to similar test examples.

fits_no_version.finding: With fixed representations learned from the full CIFAR-100 dataset, only 38 examples exceed the 0.25 memorization threshold when retraining linear classifiers, compared with 18,099 when retraining full ResNet50 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Much of example-level label memorization is encoded in learned representations before the final classification layer.

record.problems: The core removal curves in Fig. 2 are figure-only in the supplied text, with no exact values recoverable. The CIFAR-100 removal result is based on 100 random runs; ImageNet uses 5 trials. The paper does not test the claim's random-label or explicit-regularization conditions.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying reported result rows were left out. Figure 7 architecture consistency metrics and Fig. 8 linear-model comparison are not rows for the claim versions, which concern random-label fitting or regularization and true-label generalization; they concern the paper's memorization/influence estimation method.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test error across random-label corruption fractions.

Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them preserves generalization on true labels. Using augmentation without an ablation tests neither clause.
The temporal order of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Delete both proposed V5 verdicts. Generalization benefits from memorized examples do not establish V5's regularization claims, and unavailable figure values would not themselves justify limits_scope. No additional results bearing on V1–V6 were found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Whether networks fit completely random labels to near-zero training error with test error at chance, without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training-time cost of fitting random labels and convergence as corruption grows.
Fitting shuffled pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across fractions of randomly corrupted labels.

The paper uses data augmentation in its training setup but does not test whether augmentation, weight decay, or dropout prevent random-label fitting, nor whether removing regularization worsens true-label generalization. It tests removal of memorized examples and random examples and the resulting true-label test accuracy.
Whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels over training.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Remove training examples whose estimated memorization value exceeds each plotted threshold; evaluate test accuracy.

conditions.value: memorization value threshold, plotted across values

rows.uncertainty: Shaded area represents one standard deviation on 5 trials.
rows.note: The comparison also includes removing the same number of randomly chosen examples; no exact values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Example removal does not measure V5. The assertion that no numerical result is stated is incorrect: Sec. 1.1 reports that approximately 32% of ImageNet examples have memorization estimates ≥0.3; removing them costs approximately 3.4 percentage points of accuracy, versus approximately 2.6 for an equally large random subset.

relation.reason: The introduction and related work discuss random-label fitting and regularization findings, but the study does not experimentally test or use random-label fitting.

tranche.reason: The study estimates example-level memorization and influence and tests the accuracy effects of removing training examples. These experiments do not test any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: Sec. 3.3 attributes 2.38 ± 0.17 percentage points of the overall 2.54 ± 0.2-point accuracy loss to Sh0. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; the measured memorization construct is distinct from fitting a randomly labeled dataset.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: CIFAR-100, removing the high-influence memorized examples
reader_labels.reason: Removing these examples reduced test accuracy from 76.06 ± 0.28% to 73.52 ± 0.25% (R4), and accuracy on their influenced test examples from 72.14 ± 1.32% to 45.38 ± 1.45% (R5), consistent with memorized examples contributing to true-label generalization.
